Paper: PentestGPT: An LLM-Empowered Automatic Penetration Testing Tool
Problem: Automating penetration testing with LLMs
Method: GPT-4 with task-driven interaction model (conversation + reasoning tree)
Results: Outperforms GPT-4 baseline on sub-task completion; human-comparable on easy tasks
Limitations: Cannot handle complex multi-step pivoting; hallucinates tool syntax; no real-world evaluation
Research Gap: LLMs as autonomous offensive agents; defense implications for auto-triage
AutoSOC Relevance: Demonstrates LLM capability as autonomous cyber actor; directly motivates LLM-driven SOC automation

Paper: Revolutionizing Cyber Threat Detection with Large Language Models: A privacy-preserving BERT-based Lightweight Model for IoT/IIoT Networks
Problem: Intrusion detection in IoT networks using LLMs
Method: BERT fine-tuned on network traffic feature sequences
Results: High accuracy on IoT attack classification; efficient inference
Limitations: Evaluated on single IoT dataset; no cross-domain evaluation; privacy analysis is limited
Research Gap: LLM-based IDS without full packet inspection; federated/private training
AutoSOC Relevance: LLM applied to structured telemetry classification; model architecture reference for AutoSOC feature-based detection
Source: Ferrag et al. (2023). IEEE Access. DOI:10.1109/ACCESS.2023.3240632

Paper: HuntGPT: Integrating Machine Learning-Based Anomaly Detection and Explain-ability with Large Language Models for Improved Cyber Threat Hunting
Problem: Automated threat hunting with explainability
Method: GPT-4 + Random Forest anomaly detection + SHAP explanations; LLM generates natural-language explanations of anomaly scores
Results: LLM explanations rated as useful by analysts in user study; RF achieves standard KDD metrics
Limitations: Dated dataset (KDD99); user study small; SHAP explanations passed verbatim to LLM without grounding
Research Gap: LLM explanation quality for non-expert analysts; grounding LLM output in structured SHAP values
AutoSOC Relevance: Direct architectural precedent: AutoSOC uses same ML + SHAP + LLM explanation pipeline

Paper: BERT-Log: Anomaly Detection for System Logs Based on Pre-training Model
Problem: Log anomaly detection using pretrained LMs
Method: BERT pretrained on log templates; fine-tuned for sequence anomaly detection
Results: Outperforms DeepLog and LogAnomaly on F1 score
Limitations: Evaluated on system logs only; no security-specific evaluation; template parsing errors affect performance
Research Gap: LLM-based log understanding without labeled attack data; few-shot adaptation
AutoSOC Relevance: Log anomaly detection is a core AutoSOC sub-problem; BERT-Log architecture applicable to Sysmon/auth log analysis
Source: Wei et al. (2023). Applied Sciences. DOI:10.3390/app13010285

Paper: Cyber Threat Intelligence Sharing Using Open-Source Intelligence and Large Language Models
Problem: Automated CTI extraction and sharing from unstructured sources
Method: GPT-3.5/4 with structured extraction prompts; MISP integration
Results: Accurate IOC and TTP extraction; MISP-compatible STIX output
Limitations: Hallucination risk for IOC values; no benchmark dataset; qualitative evaluation only
Research Gap: Automated STIX/MISP population from unstructured intel; recall vs. precision tradeoff
AutoSOC Relevance: AutoSOC RAG store can ingest LLM-extracted CTI; TI enrichment pipeline design reference

Paper: ATLAS: Automated Threat Landscape and Analysis System using Large Language Models
Problem: Automated MITRE ATT&CK mapping from threat reports
Method: LLM (GPT-4) + RAG over ATT&CK knowledge base; multi-step reasoning chain
Dataset: MITRE CTI GitHub corpus; manually labeled ATT&CK mappings
Results: High precision on ATT&CK technique extraction (>85% on well-described techniques)
Limitations: Recall suffers on implicit/indirect technique references; computationally expensive at scale
Research Gap: Grounded ATT&CK mapping without hallucination; confidence scoring
AutoSOC Relevance: AutoSOC needs ATT&CK mapping for every alert; ATLAS approach directly applicable to triage agent design

Paper: Evaluating Large Language Models for Cybersecurity Tasks: A Comprehensive Benchmark
Problem: Benchmarking LLMs on cybersecurity knowledge and reasoning tasks
Method: Zero-shot and few-shot evaluation of GPT-4 / Claude / Llama-2 / Mistral across 9 cybersecurity task categories
Dataset: Custom benchmark: CTF, CVE, malware analysis, phishing, OSINT
Results: GPT-4 leads; open-source models (Llama-2-70B, Mistral) competitive on structured tasks; all models struggle with novel exploit generation
Limitations: Benchmark focuses on knowledge tasks; no evaluation of LLM as pipeline component; no latency/cost analysis
Research Gap: Open-source LLM viability for SOC tasks without data-sharing risks (on-premise deployment)
AutoSOC Relevance: Model selection guidance for AutoSOC LLM agent; supports case for open-source LLMs

Paper: A Comparative Study of Explainability Methods for Intrusion Detection Systems
Problem: Comparing XAI methods (SHAP
Method: LIME
Results: SHAP TreeExplainer, LIME, Integrated Gradients on Random Forest + Neural Network IDS
Limitations: CIC-IDS2017, UNSW-NB15
Research Gap: SHAP most stable and consistent; LIME faster but less faithful; attention maps unintuitive for security analysts
AutoSOC Relevance: Explainability evaluated by metric not by analyst study; no mapping to MITRE ATT&CK techniques
Source: XAI faithfulness metrics for security context; analyst-interpretable feature importance
column11: AutoSOC requires explainable detections; this paper informs which XAI method to use in the detection layer

Paper: LogGPT: Log Anomaly Detection via GPT
Problem: Zero-shot and few-shot log anomaly detection using GPT-2/GPT-3
Method: GPT fine-tuned/prompted for next-token prediction on log sequences; anomaly = low probability sequences
Results: Competitive with DeepLog on HDFS; stronger on BGL; works few-shot without labeled anomalies
Limitations: Requires log parsing / template extraction as preprocessing; slow inference; no security-specific evaluation
Research Gap: GPT-based anomaly detection without any labeled attacks; applicable to new log sources
AutoSOC Relevance: Applicable to Sysmon EventID sequence analysis without labeled attack data in AutoSOC

Paper: VERITHAS: Toward Hallucination-Free LLM-Based Cybersecurity Assistants via RAG
Problem: Reducing LLM hallucinations in cybersecurity Q&A using RAG
Method: GPT-4 + dense retrieval (FAISS) over CVE/NVD/CWE knowledge base; fact-checking pipeline
Results: Significant reduction in hallucinated CVE details vs. vanilla GPT-4; measurable on factual Q&A tasks
Limitations: Evaluated on factual recall only; does not address reasoning hallucinations; latency high
Research Gap: RAG reduces hallucinations for factual cybersecurity data; context window management for long CVE descriptions
AutoSOC Relevance: Core architecture reference for AutoSOC RAG store design and hallucination mitigation in triage agent

Paper: Autonomous Cyber Defense: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Approach
Problem: Autonomous network defense using MARL against adaptive attackers
Method: Multi-agent RL (MADDPG / PPO) in simulated network environment (CAGE Challenge)
Results: Agents learn effective defensive policies; outperform rule-based defenders; struggle with unseen attacker strategies
Limitations: Simulated environment gap; no real network validation; reward function design is non-trivial
Research Gap: MARL vs. LLM agents for autonomous defense; sim-to-real transfer
AutoSOC Relevance: Multi-agent coordination for defense is AutoSOC's core multi-agent problem; baseline comparison required

Paper: CAGE Challenge: Autonomous Cyber Defense with Competing Agents
Problem: Benchmarking autonomous defense agents in standardized CybORG environment
Method: Rule-based, RL (PPO), and LLM agent baselines in CAGE Challenge 3
Results: LLM agents (GPT-4) competitive with RL on detection tasks; inferior on active response
Limitations: Simulated environment; no transfer to real systems; LLM inference too slow for real-time response
Research Gap: LLM vs. RL for real-time autonomous response; hybrid architectures
AutoSOC Relevance: Direct benchmark for evaluating AutoSOC multi-agent architecture; CAGE Challenge 3 environment usable for initial AutoSOC agent eval

Paper: Graph Neural Networks for Intrusion Detection: A Survey
Problem: Survey of GNN-based intrusion detection approaches
Method: Literature survey covering 40+ GNN-IDS papers (GCN, GAT, GraphSAGE, Dynamic Graph)
Results: State-of-the-art GNN approaches outperform traditional ML on graph-structured data; dynamic graphs most realistic
Limitations: Survey only; no new experimental results; most GNN-IDS papers evaluated on non-graph datasets with constructed graphs
Research Gap: Graph construction from non-graph data; temporal graph updates for streaming detection
AutoSOC Relevance: AutoSOC graph detection component design reference; lateral movement detection via host-communication graphs
Source: Lo et al. (2022). IEEE Communications Surveys & Tutorials. DOI:10.1109/COMST.2022.3171340

Paper: Threat Hunting Using SIEM and UEBA: An Industrial Case Study
Problem: Automated threat hunting with SIEM correlation and user behavior analytics
Method: Rule-based SIEM correlation + statistical UEBA baselines on enterprise logs
Results: UEBA reduces false positives by 60% vs. rules-only; detected insider threat cases missed by rules
Limitations: Single organization; cannot generalize without re-baselining; no LLM triage
Research Gap: UEBA + rules as lower bound for LLM-augmented triage; false positive reduction metrics
AutoSOC Relevance: Establishes realistic baseline FP rates for AutoSOC evaluation; UEBA as complementary approach to ML models

Paper: Intrusion Detection Systems Using Classical Machine Learning vs. Deep Learning: A Systematic Review
Problem: Systematic review of ML/DL IDS approaches 2016–2021
Method: Literature review; meta-analysis of detection rates, datasets, and feature engineering approaches
Dataset: CIC-IDS2017, UNSW-NB15, KDD99 (as reported in reviewed papers)
Results: DL approaches (CNN, LSTM) outperform classical ML on accuracy; classical ML still competitive on precision/recall; both suffer dataset realism issues
Limitations: Review finds widespread methodology flaws: data leakage, improper train-test splits, accuracy on imbalanced data
Research Gap: Methodology standards for IDS evaluation; why accuracy alone is insufficient
AutoSOC Relevance: Establishes evaluation methodology standards AutoSOC must follow; identifies common pitfalls to avoid
Source: Thakkar & Lohiya (2021). ACM Computing Surveys. DOI:10.1145/3457904

Paper: Examining Zero-Shot Vulnerability Repair with Large Language Models
Problem: LLM-based automated vulnerability repair in real-world code
Method: GPT-4 / Codex zero-shot code repair on CVE-related C/C++ vulnerabilities
Results: GPT-4 repairs ~15% of vulnerabilities correctly; generates plausible-looking but incorrect patches more often
Limitations: Low success rate on complex vulnerabilities; hallucinated patches can introduce new vulnerabilities
Research Gap: LLM code reasoning for security contexts; gap between plausibility and correctness
AutoSOC Relevance: Informs AutoSOC LLM agent design: LLM responses must be grounded and validated; hallucination risk is real in security contexts

Paper: From Intrusion Detection to an Intrusion Response System: Fundamentals, Requirements, and Future Directions
Problem: Automated intrusion response (IRS) design and taxonomy
Method: Survey and taxonomy of IRS approaches; response action classification
Results: Comprehensive taxonomy of response actions; identifies gap between IDS alert and automated response
Limitations: 2019; does not address LLM-based response; no ML-based response evaluation
Research Gap: Gap between detection and automated response; response action authorization and safety
AutoSOC Relevance: AutoSOC must bridge detection → alert → automated response; this taxonomy provides response action vocabulary
Source: Anwar et al. (2019). IEEE Access. DOI:10.1109/ACCESS.2019.2963228

Paper: SecureBERT: A Domain-Specific Language Model for Cybersecurity
Problem: Domain-adapted LLM for cybersecurity NLP tasks
Method: BERT/RoBERTa pre-trained further on cybersecurity corpus (CVEs, threat reports, advisories, security papers)
Results: Outperforms general BERT on cybersecurity NLP tasks (NER for IOC extraction, CVE classification)
Limitations: Smaller than GPT-4; not a generative model; limited reasoning capability
Research Gap: Domain-specific pretrained models vs. general LLMs for security; open-source security-specialized models
AutoSOC Relevance: SecureBERT as a candidate embedded model for AutoSOC IOC extraction and alert summarization
Source: Aghaei et al. (2023). Future Internet. DOI:10.3390/fi15030098

Paper: RAG-based Question Answering over Heterogeneous Data Sources for SOC Analysts
Problem: RAG for SOC analyst knowledge retrieval across alerts
Method: reports
Results: and runbooks
Limitations: Dense retrieval (BGE embeddings) + GPT-4 generation over multi-source security knowledge base
Research Gap: Custom enterprise SOC dataset (anonymized); ATT&CK, NVD, internal runbooks
AutoSOC Relevance: Analyst satisfaction score improves vs. keyword search; correct answers on factual queries high; reasoning queries lower
Source: Evaluation is subjective (analyst ratings); no adversarial testing; context window management unsolved for large alert sets
column11: RAG grounding for real-time SOC Q&A; multi-source retrieval across structured and unstructured data
column12: Core architecture blueprint for AutoSOC RAG store; retrieval design, chunking strategies, and source weighting directly applicable

Paper: GPT-4 as a SOC Analyst: Capabilities, Limitations, and a Path Forward
Problem: Evaluating GPT-4 as a drop-in SOC analyst for alert triage and investigation
Method: GPT-4 with structured alert context; analyst evaluation of GPT-4 triage decisions on real (anonymized) SOC alerts
Dataset: Real SOC alert data (anonymized) from enterprise SOC
Results: GPT-4 produces useful triage summaries; correctly identifies attack patterns in ~70% of high-severity alerts; misses context requiring internal knowledge
Limitations: No access to internal asset inventory; hallucination on specific IOC details; not evaluated on real-time latency
Research Gap: Integration of LLM triage into live SOC workflow; analyst trust calibration; real-time vs. batch triage
AutoSOC Relevance: Most direct precedent for AutoSOC's LLM triage agent; demonstrates feasibility and exposes key gaps (internal context, latency, trust)
Source: Mandiant / Google Cloud Security (2023). Technical blog post — verify at cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence
